summary: Describes a method for identifying flows or flow groups within pseudowires so MPLS routers can spread them over equal-cost paths. Forwarding engines normally hash the MPLS label stack to balance load, so without flow identification a pseudowire would use only one path.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6391 defines an optional flow label for packets carried over a pseudowire. MPLS routers can use the label to spread separate flows across equal-cost paths, while keeping packets in each flow together.

subtitle: Add a pseudowire flow label so MPLS routers can distribute separate flows over equal-cost paths.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire may contain many flows, but routers in the MPLS network often cannot distinguish those flows and therefore cannot balance them across available paths.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress provider-edge router maps each indivisible flow to an additional MPLS label. Intermediate routers can include that label when choosing a path.
tldr.outcome: Traffic can be balanced between flows, while order is preserved only within each flow. RFC 6391 is updated by RFC 7274.

today: RFC 6391 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011. The unit metadata says RFC 7274 updates it.

sections.title: Why Balance Flows Inside a Pseudowire
sections.content:
A pseudowire normally uses one network path to preserve packet order across the emulated service. This remains the default. Some pseudowires carry many IP flows and need order preserved within each flow, but not between every flow.

Routers inside the MPLS network cannot normally inspect the pseudowire payload. The ingress provider-edge router can identify flows, so this RFC lets it add information that intermediate routers can use to distribute them over equal-cost paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire may carry many separate traffic flows. The ingress router can label those flows so the network can choose paths separately for each one.

sections.title: The Flow Label Entry
sections.content:
The flow label is carried in an additional Label Stack Entry placed between the pseudowire label and the control word, or between the pseudowire label and payload when there is no control word. The ingress router MUST assign the same flow label to packets in one indivisible flow.

The label MUST NOT be an MPLS reserved label, whose values are 0 through 15, and SHOULD remain constant while the flow exists. The RFC recommends choosing labels with high entropy to help distribute flows. The egress provider-edge router discards the flow entry unless its label is reserved. The Traffic Class field is set to zero and ignored when received.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress router adds a label for each flow, and packets in that flow keep the same label. The egress router removes the extra label after the packet reaches the far end of the pseudowire.

sections.title: Identifying Flows and Building Packets
sections.content:
The Native Service Processing function at the ingress router identifies flows or groups of flows and tells the pseudowire forwarder which flow each packet belongs to. For Ethernet, an implementation might group IP packets by source and destination address. The method for identifying a flow is outside this RFC's scope.

From the payload outward, the packet may contain a 4-octet control word, then the 4-octet flow label entry, the 4-octet pseudowire label entry, and MPLS tunnel entries of 4 octets each. The control word is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: A local function examines the service packet and assigns it to a flow. The forwarder adds the flow label alongside the existing pseudowire and tunnel information.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use Flow Labels
sections.content:
With LDP signaling, the peers use a Flow Label Sub-TLV to say whether they want to send and can receive flow labels. Its type is 0x17, its length is 4 octets, and its T and R bits respectively indicate a wish to send and an ability to receive.

A PE includes a flow label only when it has advertised T = 1 and received R = 1 from its peer. Otherwise, it MUST NOT include one. For static pseudowires without signaling, both endpoints must be configured consistently; the default is not to use flow labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint signals whether it will send labels and whether it can receive them. A direction uses flow labels only when the sender requests them and the receiver says it can accept them.

sections.title: Testing Every Path
sections.content:
A basic Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification test may use any flow label to check that the pseudowire is configured. To verify every path, a test MUST be sent over each equal-cost path, which the RFC notes may be difficult and may scale poorly.

A test sent over only one path can miss a failure specific to another path. When out-of-band VCCV is used, a Router Alert label may cause the test packet to take a different path from data with the same flow and pseudowire labels.
sections.plainLanguage: A test on one path does not confirm that every path works. Operators need a test on each equal-cost path to check all routes used by the flows.

sections.title: Limits and Suitable Traffic
sections.content:
Flow labels are useful when the ingress router can distinguish multiple flows and the pseudowire's access rate is large compared with the core link bandwidth. The mechanism does not require a new capability in the packet-switched network.

Packet order is preserved only within each flow, not across all pseudowire traffic. If sequence numbers are required, this mechanism MUST NOT be used. A single large flow gains no balancing benefit, and the RFC prohibits its use in an MPLS-TP network unless the service's integrity requirements can still be met.
sections.plainLanguage: Flow labels help when traffic contains many flows that the ingress router can identify. They do not preserve order between different flows, so services that require that ordering cannot use this method.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content:
The general security considerations for pseudowires and MPLS apply. A flow-label TTL of 1 prevents accidental forwarding based on the flow label if it reaches the top of the label stack.

IANA assigned Flow Label Sub-TLV type 0x17 with a length of 4. Congestion considerations for pseudowires also apply; non-IP flow groups require congestion avoidance for each load-balancing group.
sections.plainLanguage: The flow label has a short TTL so an incorrectly positioned label does not route a packet. Existing pseudowire congestion rules still apply.
